pos: n. (one who trips up another to take his place; the meaning of the name Jacob)
etymology: From Latin supplantare, to trip up by the sole of the foot — sub-, under, and planta, the sole. It renders Hebrew aqab, to seize by the heel, to overreach, from aqeb, the heel — the root of the name Yaaqob, Jacob.
biblical_def: He was named for what his hand was doing when he arrived: after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold on Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob. Hebrew aqab means to grab the heel, and so to trip a man and take his place. Jacob spent his youth proving the name accurate — the birthright bought from a starving brother, the blessing taken with goat skins on his arms and a lie in his mouth — and Esau's protest is the plainest definition in Scripture: he hath supplanted me these two times. Hosea, looking back centuries later, keeps both halves of the man in one verse: He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God. The supplanter became the wrestler, and the wrestler was renamed. That is the arc, and the New Testament refuses to soften the beginning of it — Jacob have I loved, said of a man whose character at that point was in his name. Jeremiah then turns the word on a whole nation: trust ye not in any brother, for every brother will utterly supplant. The heel-grasping of Genesis is not one man's flaw; it is the family trade of fallen men, and grace is what interrupted it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one that supplants; one that displaces another by stratagem or by taking his place unfairly.
webster_full: SUPPLANTER, n. One that supplants; one that undermines or displaces another.
SUPPLANT, v.t. To trip up the heels; to displace by stratagem, or by unfair means.
SUPPLANT, v.t. To overthrow; to undermine; to force away.
HEEL, n. The hind part of the foot; the part of a shoe which covers the heel.
BIRTHRIGHT, n. Any right or privilege to which a person is entitled by birth, such as an estate descendible by law to an heir.
scriptures: Genesis 25:26
And after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold on Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob: and Isaac was threescore years old when she bare them.
Hosea 12:3
He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God:
Jeremiah 9:4
Take ye heed every one of his neighbour, and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders.
Psalm 41:9
Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
corruption_summary: Ambition that displaces others is rebranded as drive and taught as a skill; Scripture names it by the grip on a heel and shows that God changed the supplanter rather than crediting his technique.
corruption_paragraphs: The supplanter is now a career type, and the vocabulary around him is admiring: driven, hungry, a closer, someone who makes his own opportunities. Jacob would have flourished in it. He identified leverage precisely — a brother faint with hunger, a father blind and near death — and moved at the right moment each time. Scripture never once praises this. It records that he fled his home in fear, was deceived by his father-in-law for twenty years, deceived in turn by his own sons over a coat, and limped for the rest of his life after the night he stopped grasping and started clinging. The method worked and cost him everything it gained.

Yet the account is not finally about Jacob's character, and reading it as a morality tale misses the point Paul makes of it. The younger was chosen before the children were born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand. God did not pick the better brother; there was no better brother. What he did was take a heel-grabber and wrestle with him until he was a prince with God, which is the only hope any supplanter has ever had. Hosea holds both facts in one sentence without embarrassment, and so should we.
roots_summary: Hebrew aqab (H6117), to seize the heel, to supplant; aqeb (H6119), the heel; Yaaqob (H3290), Jacob; bekorah (H1062), the birthright.
roots_lines: Hebrew aqab (H6117) — to take by the heel, to overreach; Esau's verb, and the root of the name.
Hebrew aqeb (H6119) — the heel; the infant's grip, and the heel bruised in the first promise of Genesis 3.
Hebrew Yaaqob (H3290) — Jacob, heel-catcher; a name that was a diagnosis.
Hebrew bekorah (H1062) — the birthright; sold for a mess of pottage, which Hebrews calls profane.
Hebrew sarah (H8280) — to strive as a prince; the root of Israel, the name that replaced the first one.
usage: “his hand took hold on Esau's heel” — named for what he was already doing.
“every brother will utterly supplant” — Jeremiah turning the word on a nation.
“hath lifted up his heel against me” — the figure carried into the betrayal of Christ.

pos: n. (an owner of large flocks; used of Mesha king of Moab)
etymology: A compound of sheep and master, formed in English to render Hebrew noqed — a sheep-breeder or flock-owner, distinct from roeh, the shepherd who tends them. The same rare word is used of Amos.
biblical_def: And Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel an hundred thousand lambs, and an hundred thousand rams, with the wool. The Hebrew noqed means an owner and breeder of flocks rather than a man who walks with them; it describes capital, not labour. Mesha's tribute is staggering — two hundred thousand animals and their fleece, paid annually — and the verse exists to explain what he had to lose when Ahab died and he rebelled. The only other man in Scripture given the same word is Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa, and who told Amaziah plainly, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit. Two sheepmasters, one a king with two hundred thousand head who sacrificed his own son on the wall when the battle turned against him, the other a working flock-owner from a hard hill town whom God took from following the sheep to prophesy against a wealthier kingdom than his own. Wealth in flocks is neutral in Scripture — Abraham, Job and David all had it. What the two sheepmasters show is that it settles nothing about a man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an owner or master of sheep; one who keeps and breeds flocks.
webster_full: SHEEPMASTER, n. An owner of sheep; a master of a flock.
HERDMAN, n. The owner or keeper of a herd or of herds; one employed in tending herds of cattle.
SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the pasture.
TRIBUTE, n. An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one prince or nation to another.
FLEECE, n. The coat of wool that covers a sheep, or that is shorn off at once.
scriptures: 2 Kings 3:4
And Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel an hundred thousand lambs, and an hundred thousand rams, with the wool.
Amos 1:1

The words of Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.
Amos 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
John 10:11
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
corruption_summary: Calling in ministry is assumed to require credential and pedigree; Amos, a sheepmaster with neither, was sent by God to a royal chapel and told its priest exactly where he had come from.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God calls whom he will from where they are. Amaziah the priest of Bethel tried to send Amos home with what he thought was an unanswerable social argument — go back to Judah, eat bread there, prophesy there, but not here, for it is the king's chapel. Amos did not defend his credentials because he had none to defend. I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and said, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel. The authority was in the sending, not in the sender's résumé.

The point cuts against a lazy conclusion as well. That God called a herdman does not mean he despises training; the same Scripture requires an elder to be apt to teach, holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers. Amos, for all his hills and sycomores, produced a book of ferocious literary and theological order. What is excluded is not learning but the assumption that a pedigree confers a commission, and the corresponding assumption that a man without one has nothing to say.
roots_summary: Hebrew noqed (H5349), a sheep-breeder or flock-owner; roeh (H7462), a shepherd; tso'n (H6629), the flock; Greek poimen (G4166), a shepherd.
roots_lines: Hebrew noqed (H5349) — an owner and breeder of sheep; used only of Mesha and of Amos.
Hebrew roeh (H7462) — one who pastures a flock; the ordinary shepherd word, used of David and of the LORD.
Hebrew tso'n (H6629) — small cattle, sheep and goats; the standing measure of wealth in the patriarchs.
Hebrew boqer (H951) — a herdman; Amos' own word for his trade before Amaziah.
Greek poimen (G4166) — a shepherd; I am the good shepherd, and the root of the pastoral office.
usage: “Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster” — wealth measured in two hundred thousand head.
“I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son” — the credential Amos did not have.
“the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” — what no owner of flocks would do.

pos: n. (one who carries out a death sentence; the man sent for the head of John the Baptist)
etymology: From Latin exsequi, to follow out, carry through — an executioner is one who follows an order to its end. In Mark it renders Greek spekoulator, a Latin loanword: a speculator, a guardsman of the household attached to a ruler for such duties.
biblical_def: Mark gives the killing of John the Baptist in one unhurried sentence and then one blunt clause: immediately the king sent an executioner, and commanded his head to be brought: and he went and beheaded him in the prison. The Greek word is a Latin military term for a bodyguard used as a headsman. Everything in the account is small, domestic and horrifying: a birthday supper, a dancing girl, an oath made in front of guests that Herod was too proud to break, a mother's grudge, and a man who had told a king the truth about his marriage lying in a cell below. Nobody in the room intended a martyrdom. Herod was exceeding sorry, Mark says, and did it anyway for his oath's sake, and for their sakes which sat with him. The same office appears in the Old Testament under the title captain of the guard — Potiphar held it, and Arioch, who was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon and was met by Daniel with counsel and wisdom. Arioch's errand was stopped; the one sent for John was not. Christ's verdict on the man in the cell had already been given: among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who executes; one who inflicts a capital punishment in pursuance of a legal warrant.
webster_full: EXECUTIONER, n. One who executes; one who inflicts a capital punishment in pursuance of a legal warrant.
EXECUTION, n. The act of signing a sentence of death; the infliction of capital punishment.
BEHEAD, v.t. To cut off the head; to sever the head from the body with a cutting instrument.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
GUARD, n. A man or body of men occupied in preserving a person or place from attack or injury.
scriptures: Mark 6:27
And immediately the king sent an executioner, and commanded his head to be brought: and he went and beheaded him in the prison,
Daniel 2:14
Then Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom to Arioch the captain of the king's guard, which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon:
Genesis 37:36
And the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh's, and captain of the guard.
John 10:11
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
corruption_summary: An unlawful oath is treated as binding, and cowardice in front of witnesses passes for integrity; Herod kept his word and murdered a prophet, and Scripture calls the keeping of that promise no virtue at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Herod's excuse is the one worth examining, because it still works on people. He had sworn, and the guests had heard him, and a man who breaks his word in public is nothing. Mark reports him exceeding sorry and reports the beheading in the same breath. Scripture does not credit the consistency. A promise to do what God forbids has no binding force; the law itself provided that a rash vow be confessed and atoned for rather than performed, and Christ later cut the whole apparatus down — swear not at all, but let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay. Herod could have broken an oath or broken a commandment. He chose to look steady in front of his dinner guests.

The second corruption is quieter and belongs to the executioner. He is the only man in the story without a motive: no grudge, no oath, no vanity — simply an order and a prison. Scripture never treats the chain of command as a defence. The midwives of Egypt disobeyed a king, Daniel's friends refused a furnace, Peter and John answered the council that we ought to obey God rather than men. A man who follows an order to its end is called by a name in English that means exactly that, and the name does not absolve him.
roots_summary: Greek spekoulator (G4688), a guardsman used as a headsman; apokephalizo (G607), to behead; Hebrew tabbach (H2876), a slaughterer or bodyguard; shebuah (H7621), an oath.
roots_lines: Greek spekoulator (G4688) — a Latin loanword, a household guard employed for executions; used once.
Greek apokephalizo (G607) — to cut off the head; used of John in all three synoptic accounts.
Hebrew tabbach (H2876) — a slaughterer, hence a bodyguard; Potiphar's title, captain of the guard.
Hebrew shebuah (H7621) — an oath; Herod's reason, and no reason at all.
Greek horkos (G3727) — an oath; for his oath's sake, and for their sakes which sat with him.
usage: “the king sent an executioner” — the order that ended John's ministry.
“which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon” — the same errand, stopped.
“captain of the guard” — the Old Testament title for the office.

pos: n. (one who tends a garden; what Mary supposed the risen Christ to be)
etymology: From Old French jardinier, from jardin, a garden — ultimately from a Germanic root meaning an enclosure. In John it renders Greek kepouros, literally a garden-keeper, from kepos, garden, and ouros, a watcher.
biblical_def: Mary Magdalene stands weeping outside an empty tomb, and the risen Lord asks her why she weeps and whom she seeks. She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away. It is one of the great near-misses of Scripture, and the mistake is more fitting than she knew. There was a garden in the place where he was crucified, and in the garden a new sepulchre; the man she took for its keeper was the one who had planted the first garden and put a man in it to dress it and to keep it. The whole story of Scripture runs from a garden where a man was driven out to a garden where a woman was told, go to my brethren. Jesus takes garden language for himself constantly: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman; the dresser of the vineyard pleading one more year for a barren fig tree; the sower, the seed, the harvest, the wheat and the tares. Mary was not wrong about his trade. She was only wrong about which garden he was keeping, and how recently he had come out of the ground.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one whose occupation is to make, tend and dress a garden; one skilled in gardening.
webster_full: GARDENER, n. One whose occupation is to make, tend and dress a garden.
GARDEN, n. A piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, fruits, flowers or plants of any kind.
DRESSER, n. One who dresses; one who prunes and tends vines or trees.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; the place in which the dead body of a human being is interred.
HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground.
scriptures: John 20:15

Jesus saith unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou? She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away.
John 15:1
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Luke 13:7
Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?
Genesis 3:23
Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.
corruption_summary: The resurrection is treated as a symbol of renewal that the seasons already teach; John reports a woman who could not find a body, argued with a stranger about where it had been moved, and then heard her own name.
corruption_paragraphs: Spring is the standard modern reading of Easter: life returns, as it always does, and the resurrection is the church's way of saying so. John's account resists this at every point. Mary is not meditating on renewal; she is looking for a corpse and offering to carry it herself. The tomb is a real tomb with grave clothes lying in it and a napkin folded separately. The conversation is mundane to the point of awkwardness — she takes him for staff and asks about logistics. Nothing here is a seasonal metaphor. Paul stakes everything on the difference: if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain, ye are yet in your sins, and we are of all men most miserable.

The fitting thing about Mary's error, though, should not be lost to the argument. He was in a garden, and he does keep gardens. He planted one and walked in it in the cool of the day; he calls his Father the husbandman and himself the vine; he stood in another garden the night before and sweat as it were great drops of blood. The gospel begins with a man driven out of a garden and turns, at a grave in a garden, when a gardener says one word — Mary — and she knows him.
roots_summary: Greek kepouros (G2780), a garden-keeper; kepos (G2779), a garden; georgos (G1092), a husbandman or vinedresser; Hebrew gan (H1588), a garden.
roots_lines: Greek kepouros (G2780) — a keeper of a garden; used once in Scripture, and mistakenly.
Greek kepos (G2779) — a garden; John notes there was one in the place where he was crucified.
Greek georgos (G1092) — a tiller of the soil, a vinedresser; my Father is the husbandman.
Hebrew gan (H1588) — a garden, an enclosure; Eden, and the garden of Gethsemane's counterpart.
Hebrew abad (H5647) — to work, to serve, to till; the man was put in the garden to do it.
usage: “supposing him to be the gardener” — a mistake more fitting than she knew.
“my Father is the husbandman” — the trade claimed in plain words.
“to till the ground from whence he was taken” — the first man sent out of the first garden.

pos: n. (a youth not yet full grown; Saul's word for David after Goliath fell)
etymology: From strip, in the sense of a long thin slip of wood, with the diminutive -ling — a stripling is a lad as slender as a strip. It renders Hebrew elem, a young man, used only twice in Scripture.
biblical_def: The word appears in the strangest possible place. Goliath is dead, David is walking back with the head in his hand, and Saul — who had armed him personally an hour earlier — turns to Abner and says, Enquire thou whose son the stripling is. A stripling: a slip of a lad, not a man yet. It is the third time the chapter has measured David that way. Saul had said, thou art not able to go against this Philistine, for thou art but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth; and the Philistine, when he looked about and saw him, disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance. Everyone in the story agrees on the assessment and everyone is wrong about what it means, because none of them heard the argument David made to Saul — the lion and the bear, thy servant slew both, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God. Paul writes the same principle to a young minister facing older men: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers — not, insist on your standing, but give them nothing to despise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a youth in the state of adolescence, or just passing from boyhood to manhood; a lad.
webster_full: STRIPLING, n. A youth in the state of adolescence, or just passing from boyhood to manhood; a lad.
YOUTH, n. The part of life that succeeds to childhood; a young person; a young man.
DISDAIN, v.t. To think unworthy; to deem worthless; to scorn; to contemn.
RUDDY, a. Of a red color; of a lively flesh color, or the color of the human skin in high health.
EXAMPLE, n. A pattern; a copy; a model; that which is proposed to be imitated.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 17:56
And the king said, Enquire thou whose son the stripling is.
1 Samuel 17:33
And Saul said to David, Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him: for thou art but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth.
1 Samuel 17:42
And when the Philistine looked about, and saw David, he disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance.
1 Timothy 4:12
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
corruption_summary: Youth is flattered as a qualification in itself or dismissed as disqualifying; Scripture does neither — it tells the young man to be an example and tells the church not to despise him.
corruption_paragraphs: The church in the West has spent a generation treating youth as an asset to be marketed — younger leadership, younger music, a younger look — as though the calendar conferred insight. Scripture is unsentimental about this. It gives the office of elder its name from age, requires that a man not be a novice lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil, and commands the younger to submit themselves unto the elder. David, for all his courage, was not made king that afternoon; he went back to the sheep, and waited years, and refused twice to take the throne by force when it was within reach of his hand.

The opposite error is just as real, and Paul wrote against it. Let no man despise thy youth was addressed to a church, not only to Timothy, and the remedy Paul prescribes is not a demand for respect but a life: be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity. Six areas, all observable. Saul asked whose son the stripling was because a boy had just done what the whole army would not. The question a church should be asking about its young men is the same one — not how old is he, but what has he already done in the fields where nobody was watching.
roots_summary: Hebrew elem (H5958), a young man or stripling; naar (H5288), a youth or servant lad; Greek neotes (G3503), youth; kataphroneo (G2706), to despise.
roots_lines: Hebrew elem (H5958) — a stripling; used only twice, both times of David in this chapter.
Hebrew naar (H5288) — a boy, a lad, a servant; the word Saul and Goliath both use of him.
Greek neotes (G3503) — youth; what Timothy was told not to let men despise.
Greek kataphroneo (G2706) — to think down upon, to despise; the same verb used of despising the riches of God's goodness.
Greek tupos (G5179) — a pattern, an example; the remedy Paul gives for being despised.
usage: “Enquire thou whose son the stripling is” — asked with a giant's head in view.
“thou art but a youth, and he a man of war” — the reasonable assessment.
“Let no man despise thy youth” — and the six-part answer that follows it.

pos: n. (one not in bondage; in Paul, the standing of a slave who belongs to Christ)
etymology: Old English freomann, a free man — one possessing the rights of a citizen, as against a bondman. It renders Greek apeleutheros, a freedman: not one born free, but one who was a slave and has been set at liberty by his master.
biblical_def: Paul writes to a church with slaves and masters in the same room, and he does not begin by changing their circumstances. He changes the address. For he that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord's freeman: likewise also he that is called, being free, is Christ's servant. The Greek for freeman is apeleutheros, a freedman — a man who was owned and has been manumitted. Paul does not tell the slave he is already free in some abstract sense; he tells him whose freedman he is, and tells the free man in the next clause that he is Christ's slave. Both statuses are inverted at once, and neither man leaves the conversation with a reason to look down on the other. This is not indifference to bondage — Paul says in the same passage, if thou mayest be made free, use it rather, and he sends Onesimus back to Philemon asking that he be received not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved. What he refuses is the idea that a man's standing before God waits on his standing in society. The day is coming when every bondman and every free man will hide together in the rocks. Between now and then, if the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who enjoys liberty, or who is not subject to the will of another; one who is not a slave or vassal.
webster_full: FREEMAN, n. One who enjoys liberty, or who is not subject to the will of another; one not a slave or vassal.
FREEMAN, n. One who enjoys or is entitled to a franchise or peculiar privilege.
BONDMAN, n. A man slave, or one bound to service without wages.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit, without any restraint but the laws of nature.
MANUMIT, v.t. To release from slavery; to liberate from personal bondage or servitude; to free.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 7:22
For he that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord's freeman: likewise also he that is called, being free, is Christ's servant.
John 8:36
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
Galatians 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Revelation 6:15

And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains;
corruption_summary: Freedom is defined as the absence of obligation — no master, no rule, no claim — while Paul defines it as a change of owner, and makes Christ's freedman and Christ's servant the same man.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern definition of liberty is negative: freedom is what is left when nobody is telling you what to do. Paul never once uses the word that way. His freeman is a freedman, a man who has been bought out of one ownership into another, and the very next clause makes the free man Christ's slave. There is no third category in his letters. Ye were the servants of sin, he writes, but now being made free from sin and become servants to God, ye have your fruit unto holiness. The question Scripture asks is never whether a man serves, but whom, and Christ's yoke is the only one described as easy and his burden the only one called light.

Galatians shows the other danger, which is to take the liberty and walk straight back into a yoke — in that case circumcision and the law, in ours whatever set of rules or approvals a man cannot live without. Paul's command is to stand fast, and he immediately guards it from the opposite abuse: use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another. Peter says the same, as free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God. A freeman in the New Testament is recognisable by two things at once — he will not be enslaved again, and he willingly serves.
roots_summary: Greek apeleutheros (G558), a freedman; eleutheros (G1658), free; doulos (G1401), a bondservant; eleutheria (G1657), liberty.
roots_lines: Greek apeleutheros (G558) — a manumitted slave; used once, and of a believing servant.
Greek eleutheros (G1658) — free, not a slave; ye shall be free indeed.
Greek doulos (G1401) — a bondservant; Paul's own preferred self-description in his letters.
Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty; the thing Galatians commands believers to stand fast in.
Greek agorazo (G59) — to buy in the market; ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men.
usage: “being a servant, is the Lord's freeman” — the address changed before the circumstance.
“ye shall be free indeed” — the only freedom Christ claims to give.
“every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves” — the distinction ending together.

pos: n. (an attendant or serving man; the one who questioned Elisha's order to feed a hundred)
etymology: From Latin servire, to serve, through Old French servitour — an older and more formal English word than servant, meaning an attendant on a person. It renders Hebrew mesharet, a minister or personal attendant, the same word used of Joshua serving Moses.
biblical_def: A man came from Baalshalisha with twenty loaves of barley and full ears of corn, and Elisha said, Give unto the people, that they may eat. There were a hundred men. And his servitor said, What, should I set this before an hundred men? It is an honest objection from a man holding the bread, and it is the exact objection Andrew would make centuries later over five barley loaves: there is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many? Barley in both cases, the bread of the poor. Elisha does not argue arithmetic. He repeats the order and adds a word from the LORD: Give the people, that they may eat: for thus saith the LORD, They shall eat, and shall leave thereof. And so he set it before them, and they did eat, and left thereof, according to the word of the LORD. The servitor's question was not wicked; it was the sane assessment of what he had in his hands. What he had not weighed was the word attached to it. Paul's description of the office covers the same ground: let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God — a steward does not have to own the supply, only to distribute it as ordered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a servant; an attendant; one who serves or waits on another.
webster_full: SERVITOR, n. A servant; an attendant.
SERVITOR, n. One who acts under another; a follower or adherent.
STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants and provide for the table.
MINISTER, n. An agent; anyone who performs the will of another; a servant.
BARLEY, n. A species of grain used especially for making malt, and the bread of the poorer sort.
scriptures: 2 Kings 4:43
And his servitor said, What, should I set this before an hundred men? He said again, Give the people, that they may eat: for thus saith the LORD, They shall eat, and shall leave thereof.
2 Kings 4:44
So he set it before them, and they did eat, and left thereof, according to the word of the LORD.
John 6:9
There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?
1 Corinthians 4:1
Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.
corruption_summary: Ministry is measured by what the minister can visibly supply, so small resources are read as a verdict on the work; the servitor was told to distribute what he had because a word had been spoken over it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a steward's duty is set by his orders and not by his inventory. The servitor was right about the bread and wrong about the situation, because the resource was no longer the only relevant fact: thus saith the LORD, They shall eat, and shall leave thereof. Small congregations, thin budgets and short staffs produce the same honest objection every week, and the answer is the same — set it before them. It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful, which is a measure of obedience rather than of supply.

The second half must be held with the first, or this becomes an excuse for presumption. Elisha did not manufacture a promise; he received one and passed it on, and the narrator is careful to say the men ate and left according to the word of the LORD. Where no such word has been given, a steward is simply a steward, and Scripture expects him to count the cost, to provide things honest, and not to build a tower he cannot finish. The servitor's error was not prudence. It was assuming that prudence had the last word when God had already spoken after it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mesharet (H8334), a personal attendant or minister; lechem (H3899), bread; Greek huperetes (G5257), an under-rower or servant; oikonomos (G3623), a steward.
roots_lines: Hebrew mesharet (H8334) — an attendant; the same word used of Joshua the minister of Moses.
Hebrew seorah (H8184) — barley; the poor man's grain, in both feeding miracles.
Greek huperetes (G5257) — literally an under-rower; Paul's word for ministers of Christ.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a house-manager, a steward; entrusted with what is not his own.
Greek perisseuo (G4052) — to abound, to be left over; twelve baskets after the five loaves.
usage: “What, should I set this before an hundred men?” — the honest arithmetic.
“They shall eat, and shall leave thereof” — the word attached to the bread.
“stewards of the mysteries of God” — distributing what is not their own.

pos: n. (one who cultivates the ground; the trade of Cain)
etymology: From Old English tilian, to strive after, to cultivate — the same root as till in the sense of labour. It renders Hebrew oved adamah, a server of the ground, from abad, to work or serve, and adamah, the ground from which Adam was taken.
biblical_def: And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. Two trades, introduced in a single verse, and the text gives no hint that one is better. Tilling was the first commission — there was not a man to till the ground before Adam was made, and when the man was driven out of Eden it was to till the ground from whence he was taken. Cain took up his father's work. What went wrong was not the trade but the offering, and the New Testament says why: by faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain. Then the ground itself became the instrument of the sentence. God, who had cursed the ground for Adam's sake, tells Cain: When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth. The tiller is sentenced to till soil that will not answer him. From that point Scripture treats the ground as a witness — the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground — and the curse stands over all human labour until the last Adam, buried in the earth, comes out of it in a garden.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who tills; a husbandman; a cultivator; one who ploughs or cultivates the earth.
webster_full: TILLER, n. One who tills; a husbandman; a cultivator.
TILL, v.t. To labor; to cultivate; to plow and prepare for seed, and to dress crops.
TILLAGE, n. The operation, practice or art of tilling and preparing land for seed, and keeping the ground free from weeds.
HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground.
VAGABOND, n. A vagrant; one who wanders from town to town without any settled habitation.
scriptures: Genesis 4:2
And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.
Genesis 2:5

And every plant of the field before it was in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew: for the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground.
Genesis 3:23
Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.
Genesis 4:12
When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.
corruption_summary: Work is treated either as a curse to be escaped or as the source of a man's worth; Genesis gives tillage before the fall as a commission and after it as a labour under a curse, and neither reading survives the text.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors about work both misread Genesis 2 and 3. The first says labour is a consequence of the fall, something to be minimized and finally escaped — a view that makes retirement the goal of life and treats the working years as a sentence served. But Adam was put in the garden to dress it and to keep it before there was any sin in the world; the commission is older than the curse. What the fall introduced was thorns, sweat, frustration and a ground that does not answer honest effort. The work itself was a gift, and remains one.

The second error makes a man's work his identity, so that his value rises and falls with his output. Cain is the warning here. His offering was of the fruit of the ground — his own labour, brought to God — and when it was not respected he was wroth and his countenance fell, and God asked him why. A man whose worth is his yield has no answer when the yield fails, and the ground had already been told not to give Cain its strength. Paul settles the question for Christians from another direction entirely: whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward.
roots_summary: Hebrew abad (H5647), to work, serve, till; adamah (H127), the ground; Qayin (H7014), Cain; arar (H779), to curse.
roots_lines: Hebrew abad (H5647) — to work or serve; the same verb for tilling soil and for serving God.
Hebrew adamah (H127) — the ground; the word from which Adam is taken, and to which he returns.
Hebrew koach (H3581) — strength; the ground shall not yield Cain her strength.
Hebrew arar (H779) — to curse; the ground cursed for Adam's sake, and Cain cursed from the ground.
Hebrew na and nad (H5128) — a fugitive and a vagabond; the sentence on the first tiller who shed blood.
usage: “Cain was a tiller of the ground” — his father's trade, taken up without comment.
“there was not a man to till the ground” — the commission older than the curse.
“it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength” — the sentence laid in the soil.

pos: n. (one who pours out blood; Ezekiel's name for the violent man)
etymology: From Old English sceadan, to divide, separate, pour out. In Ezekiel it renders a participle of Hebrew shaphak, to pour out — used of pouring out blood, and also of pouring out one's heart before God.
biblical_def: Ezekiel 18 is the chapter that dismantles the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes and children's teeth being set on edge. It works through three generations — a just man, then his violent son, then that son's righteous son — and the middle man is introduced this way: If he beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, and that doeth the like to any one of these things. The soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son. The shedder stands or falls on his own account. Why blood is treated this way in Scripture is stated once, early, and never withdrawn: Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man. The reason is not the value of human life in the abstract but the image stamped on it; to destroy a man is to strike at the likeness of God. Among the six things the LORD hates and the seventh that is an abomination, Proverbs lists hands that shed innocent blood, and Isaiah says of a whole society, their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who sheds or pours out; one who spills, as blood; one that causes to flow.
webster_full: SHEDDER, n. One who sheds or causes to flow; as a shedder of blood.
SHED, v.t. To pour out; to effuse; to spill; to suffer to flow out.
INNOCENT, a. Free from guilt; not having done wrong or violated any law.
MURDER, n. The act of unlawfully killing a human being with premeditated malice.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing; a likeness.
scriptures: Ezekiel 18:10
If he beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, and that doeth the like to any one of these things,
Genesis 9:6
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
Proverbs 6:17
A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood,
Isaiah 59:7
Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood: their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; wasting and destruction are in their paths.
corruption_summary: The worth of human life is grounded in capacity, wantedness or quality of life, which leaves every weak life negotiable; Genesis grounds it in the image of God and gives no other reason.
corruption_paragraphs: Every modern framework for valuing human life makes the value contingent on something the person has — consciousness, viability, autonomy, a projected quality of life, or the desire of somebody else that they exist. Each of these can be measured, and therefore each can be found insufficient, which is why the unborn, the very old, the disabled and the dying are the first to be reasoned out of protection. Genesis 9:6 gives a different ground and only one: for in the image of God made he man. The image is not a capacity a man exercises but a stamp he bears, and it is not diminished by age, injury, or inconvenience to anyone.

Scripture's severity about bloodshed follows from that, and so does its mercy. The same God who says whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed, appointed cities of refuge for the man who killed unawares, and distinguished carefully between murder and manslaughter. And the same Ezekiel who names the shedder says in the same chapter: have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live? Manasseh filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and repented, and was heard. Paul consented to Stephen's death, and was made an apostle. There is blood that speaketh better things than that of Abel.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaphak (H8210), to pour out; dam (H1818), blood; naqi (H5355), innocent; tselem (H6754), image.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaphak (H8210) — to pour out; used of shedding blood and of pouring out the heart before God.
Hebrew dam (H1818) — blood; the life of the flesh is in the blood.
Hebrew naqi (H5355) — clean, innocent; the blood Proverbs says God hates to see shed.
Hebrew tselem (H6754) — image; the single reason Genesis gives for the sanctity of human life.
Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to murder; the verb of the sixth commandment, distinguished from lawful killing.
usage: “a robber, a shedder of blood” — the middle man of Ezekiel's three generations.
“for in the image of God made he man” — the reason, and the only one given.
“hands that shed innocent blood” — among the things the LORD hates.

pos: n. (one who brings calamity on a people; Ahab's accusation against Elijah)
etymology: From Latin turbulare, to disturb, from turba, a crowd or tumult, through Old French troubler. In 1 Kings it renders Hebrew akar, to stir up muddy water, and so to bring ruin — the root behind the valley of Achor.
biblical_def: Three years of drought, and when Ahab finally meets the prophet who announced it he opens with an accusation: Art thou he that troubleth Israel? Elijah's answer is one of the great refusals in Scripture, and it does not hedge. I have not troubled Israel; but thou, and thy father's house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the LORD, and thou hast followed Baalim. The man who announced the drought is not the man who caused it. Hebrew akar means to stir up water until it is undrinkable, and it names the valley where Achan was stoned — Joshua said to him, Why hast thou troubled us? the LORD shall trouble thee this day, and the place was called Achor after it. So the word carries a settled meaning: the troubler of a people is the one whose sin brings judgment on the whole, not the one who names it. Paul uses it the same way of men unsettling the Galatian churches — there be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ — and the troublers there are the ones adding to the gospel, not Paul who was resisting them. The accusation always runs the same direction, and so does the truth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who troubles or disturbs; one who afflicts or molests; a disturber of peace or order.
webster_full: TROUBLER, n. One who troubles or disturbs; one who afflicts or molests; a disturber.
TROUBLE, v.t. To agitate; to disturb; to put into confused motion.
TROUBLE, v.t. To afflict; to grieve; to distress; to perplex.
DISTURB, v.t. To stir; to move; to discompose; to excite from a state of rest or tranquillity.
PERVERT, v.t. To turn from truth, propriety, or from its proper purpose; to distort from its true use or end.
scriptures: 1 Kings 18:17
And it came to pass, when Ahab saw Elijah, that Ahab said unto him, Art thou he that troubleth Israel?
1 Kings 18:18
And he answered, I have not troubled Israel; but thou, and thy father's house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the LORD, and thou hast followed Baalim.
Joshua 7:25
And Joshua said, Why hast thou troubled us? the LORD shall trouble thee this day. And all Israel stoned him with stones, and burned them with fire, after they had stoned them with stones.
Galatians 1:7
Which is not another; but there be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ.
corruption_summary: The one who names a sin is treated as the cause of the trouble it brings; Elijah answers the charge by naming who actually forsook the commandments, and Scripture keeps the word for those whose sin brings the judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Ahab's move is perfectly modern: locate the disturbance in the person who mentioned the problem. It is effective because it is partly true — things were calm before Elijah came, and they were not calm afterward. Every church that has ever disciplined a member, every man who has told a friend the truth about his life, has met the same accounting. Elijah's reply is worth memorizing for its structure as much as its courage: he denies the charge flatly, then states the actual cause, then names the responsible party to his face. He does not apologize for the drought, and he does not pretend it was pleasant.

The word must not be turned into a licence for quarrelsomeness, because Scripture also knows real troublers inside the church. The Galatian troublers were not plain speakers; they were men adding requirements to the gospel and unsettling young believers, and Paul says let them be accursed. Proverbs says a froward man soweth strife, and that he that troubleth his own house shall inherit the wind. The test is not whether a man causes disturbance but what he is disturbing it over: Elijah over the commandments of the LORD forsaken, Paul over the gospel of Christ perverted. Trouble raised over anything less is just trouble.
roots_summary: Hebrew akar (H5916), to stir up, to trouble, to bring ruin; Akor (H5911), Achor; Greek tarasso (G5015), to agitate; metastrepho (G3344), to pervert.
roots_lines: Hebrew akar (H5916) — to stir water into mud; used of Achan, of Elijah's accusers, and of Jephthah's daughter.
Hebrew Akor (H5911) — Achor, trouble; the valley named for Achan, and promised as a door of hope in Hosea.
Greek tarasso (G5015) — to agitate, to trouble; used of the Galatian troublers and of the Lord's own soul.
Greek metastrepho (G3344) — to turn about, to pervert; what the troublers were doing to the gospel.
Hebrew Baalim (H1168) — the Baals; what Elijah names as the true cause of the drought.
usage: “Art thou he that troubleth Israel?” — the accusation aimed at the messenger.
“I have not troubled Israel; but thou” — the charge returned with the evidence.
“there be some that trouble you” — the word used of real troublers in a church.
